Hi, I opened a PR cslib#802 that defines a multi-tape non-deterministic TM. It's defined as an initial configuration and a transition relation, analogous to the transition function in a deterministic TM.

The PR defines an LTS over the configurations of the non-deterministic TM in order to define computation in time and space.

Then there is a proof that the current definition of the deterministic multi-tape TM is trivially a non-deterministic multi-tape TM.

A natural next step I'm working on is to define the deterministic multi-tape TM as a specialization of the non-deterministic one, which fits cleanly given how the NTM is defined.

Any feedback and thoughts on the PR are welcome :)

Github is currently not working for me, so I'll comment here for now.

Thanks for the pull request! I haven't looked at it too much in detail, but I think I understand the concept. Basing it on LTSs will look a bit alien to people used to the way NTMs are introduced in textbooks, and I'm also not sure that the output symbol is a natural label (although I see it working and also don't have a better idea right now).

In general, I think it would be nice if a List of configurations would be the same as a computation. Then we could re-use the machinery from RelatesInSteps.lean and the number of steps is just the length of the list. At the same time, I myself recently removed the output from Cnf which makes it impossible to derive a unique output string from a list of configurations.
On the other hand, the main reason I removed it was to be able to count the number of reachable configurations. In the same PR, though, I also extracted a "storage configuration" which is the fields of the configuration without the input head position. So we need to be able to speak about a subset of the fields already.
After all, the output is written on a tape, so one could argue that it should be part of the configuration.
Maybe we should put it back after all? That would allow us to instantly "read off" the output from the halting configuration.

There are just some ideas for now, what do you think, @Aviv Bar Natan ?

I think it's fine that we add back the output tape, but then call the structure "Snapshot" or something, not Cfg. Because Cfg should be the information required for taking a step.

I agree that if we add the output tape back then defining a computation as a list of configurations that "relate in steps" would be natural.
Whatever you think is better, you removed it in the first place so I guess there was a good reason.

Two more things:

  1. Can we define compuations using the API of graphs in mathlib? I think it will be the most beneficial, and it feels like everything we're doing is actually walking on the configurations graph.
  2. Anyway, I think that we can just decide any of the options, and after that we prove Savitch it will be a nice milestone for revising the definitions. A refactor won't be too hard

While working on https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/779 I also wanted to re-use results from Mathlib's graph API. I heard that it is currently being refactored, but as it stands now, it's unfortunately not usable: We need directed graphs that allow self-edges, and this combination just does not exist. But the good thing about it: Such graphs are exactly the same as pure relations (if we allow all elements of a type as the vertex set). So a walk in such a graph is just List.IsChain. So the API is already there, just not under the term "graph".

About the naming: I think "configuration" is still the right term: Textbooks usually use that term for the instantaneous description of everything about the Turing machine, and the output tape is part of that even if it's not needed to compute the next step. The step relation would be a relation on Cfg (instead of a relation between Snapshot and Cfg, which is also quite natural.

If you want, I can do the change on top of current main, but you can also do it in your PR, as you prefer.

Sorry, now that I look again, Mathlib's Digraph actually does permit self-loops. So it is exactly what we need. Maybe what I was not able to find was walks / paths on such graphs, which do exist but in the name of List.IsChain.
Ok so let's do it - add the output tape to Cfg. But note that the relation is still between a Cfg and a OutTransition, not between Cfgs
I don't really understand - which relation?

About the graph, then let's do it!
Order of implementation (each one will be a PR):

  1. refactor Cfg to have the tput tape
  2. Adding the non-deterministic TM with graph API vs RelateInSteps API
  3. Defining the deterministic machine as a special case of the non-determinisrtric machine?

Yes, I think we should have step 3 as well. A deterministic TM should be a special case of a nondeterministic TM plus constructors that take a transition function and a way to get sequence of configurations instead of the graph of reachable configurations.
Oh ok I've got confused with he Tr relation. Yeah I agree the Step relation will be over Cfgs
Ok cool I'll now implement 1,2 I have time
I reviewed https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/819 and only have some minor comments.
Cool I'll look at it. I'm doing now the Non-deterministic refactor as we decided

1. Refactoring Cfg to include the output: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/819
  2. Defining non-deterministic TM via RelSeries which makes it very clean and the list of configurations can be deived by a built-in toList: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/820

After consulting with @Christian Reitwiessner I created a PR that improves the names of the TransitionOut structure to reflect the action on the work tapes, the state and the output:
https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/827/changes

Hello,
I noticed that we have the following functions:

SingleTapeTM.step : Cfg → Option Cfg -- none if cfg is halted
MultiTapeTM.step : Cfg → Cfg -- halted cfg maps to itself

…and matchingly, we can do a Step that does nothing in MultiTapeNTM after computation stops – leading to the unusual situation that ComputesInExactTime for MultiTapeNTM always allows one to add arbitrarily many steps, making it possible to prove something like this:

theorem make_more_steps (h : ComputesInExactTime tm i o k) : ComputesInExactTime tm i o (k+1) := ⋯

Thus I argue this corresponds more to the intutive notion of '≤' than '=' (like the word "exact" would seem to imply) in terms of time consumed. MultiTapeTM.ComputesInTimeAndSpace behaves likewise wrt. time (≤) but not wrt. space (=) (like is documented).

Is there some reason this behavior was chosen, and also why it is not consistent with SingleTapeTM?

On the same note, SingleTapeTM / Relation uses different terminology (WithinTime, InTime), which I find overall quite confusing.

Thanks for the observation! You are right, it should not be called "InExactTime". Please create a pull request if you want. Having said that, we are currently in the process of unifying the API for nondeterministic and deterministic multi-tape Turing machines, so it might change again - but which also means that we will probably need to solve more naming problems. The relation to (and position of) single-tape TMs still has to be figured out, including the relation to mathlib's Turing machine.

What would be the correct terminology in your opinion? I would be in favour of WithinTime for consistency with Relation but introducing this distinction to this (and the deterministic variant) file would cause troube for the current InTimeAndSpace/InExactTimeAndSpace.

Btw. I just noticed we have MultiTapeTM.Nondeterministic but SingleTapeTM.NonDeterministic (capital D). :sweat_smile:

I personally don't see a semantic difference between "in time" and "within time", and I think text books use "in" (although I might misremember). Wikipedia uses "nondeterministic" as one word: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nondeterministic_Turing_machine and I think the reason is to distinguish it from the negation of "deterministic".
